It is economically distinct from margin level, dispersion and asymmetry legs because it counts the frequency of the loss state rather than measuring its depth, and it requires no volatility estimate so coverage stays near 0.12.

considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(MUL(SUB(MA(RATIO(pi, revt), 3), TS_MIN(RATIO(pi, revt), 3)), revt), ADD(che, SUB(revt, cogs))), VOL(GROWTH(revt, 1), 3))
considered.hypothesis: The share of a firm's total absorption capacity — cash plus one year of gross profit — that a single trough year would consume is the sharpest statement of fragility, and it should be assessed jointly with how likely such a trough is, which the volatility of revenue growth measures.
considered.reasoning:
The first leg is not an archived channel but the dimensional survival-multiple construct built in this same generation, so this is not a reweighting of previously combined legs: it pairs a shortfall-to-resources ratio with a shock-probability measure, which is the natural economic decomposition of expected distress into severity and likelihood. If the survival multiple carries the alpha as its cash-denominated predecessor did (-6.0%) and the volatility leg supplies the slope, this is the specification most likely to deliver both forms of evidence.

critic_notes.rationale: The conditional logic is internally consistent (NEG(coverage) > -0.10 correctly switches on when coverage < 10%) and the sign matches, but it is a fairly incremental refinement of the well-documented leverage/distress anomaly and the mass of exact zeros for non-qualifying firms will make the long leg an arbitrary, unstable mixture rather than an economically meaningful portfolio.

The ratio construction genuinely interacts two themes (cash-flow solvency and earnings instability) with a coherent default-distance interpretation and matching positive sign, but the near-zero-volatility denominator will dominate the cross-section so the signal risks collapsing into a low-earnings-volatility (quality) proxy that 1% winsorization only partly tames.

Nested SUMRANK is just an equal-weighted average of four ranks with no conditioning or interaction, and the specific inputs (retained earnings/assets, working capital/assets, liabilities/assets, cash flow) are close to a rediscovery of Altman Z / Ohlson O / Piotroski-style distress-quality composites.

Change-conditional-on-quality is a defensible construction with a consistent sign, though it sits close to known leverage-change/debt-issuance and asset-growth anomalies interacted with profitability, and the zero-valued non-qualifying majority plus signed trend values means the long leg pools deleveraging weak-cash firms with an undifferentiated zero mass.

The reversed-sign conditional is a legitimate and informative counterpart to the distress version and would sharply diagnose whether the interaction rather than the leverage level drives results, but the positive expected sign fights substantial evidence that leverage predicts returns negatively even among profitable firms, and the zero mass again weakens the short leg.

This is the standard cash-flow-statement total accruals measure (Sloan/Hribar-Collins) with the deflator swapped from assets to liabilities, which is a cosmetic rescaling rather than a cross-theme interaction and will load almost entirely on the known accruals anomaly.

The burn-time framing of cash/cogs is a reasonable and non-standard scaling and the sign logic is internally consistent, but the pi/at leg is essentially the well-known profitability anomaly and is likely to dominate the rank product, so the incremental content rests entirely on the liquidity interaction actually biting.

Despite the claim that it is "not rescaling a known anomaly," this is precisely gross profitability (Novy-Marx) with liabilities substituted for assets and a small tax adjustment, so it will be highly correlated with an established, already-published factor and the 3-year smoothing is a cosmetic rather than economic differentiator.

The coverage × liability-growth interaction is coherent and correctly signed, but both legs are individually known effects (profitability/coverage and debt-issuance/asset-growth), and the rank-product form cannot separate a genuine interaction from a simple average of two established anomalies.

The five-year gross-margin trend conditioned on cash-to-current-liabilities is an economically specific, correctly signed combination of a slow-moving quality deterioration with an explicit financing constraint, and it is the least redundant of the batch — though the trend leg overlaps somewhat with the fundamental-trends literature and 5-year windows will cost coverage.

The tax-validation story is interesting but the expression divides by gross profit, which is near zero or negative for exactly the distressed firms the signal targets, producing sign-flipping, fat-tailed ratios that RANK cannot repair; a bounded construction (e.g., txt scaled by revenue or assets) would be needed before the hypothesis is testable.

The stated hypothesis is about leverage being *conditionally* safe, but a plain rank product does not condition — it simply longs high-wcap/high-leverage and shorts low-wcap/low-leverage firms, and the expected positive sign on the dltt/at leg directly contradicts the negative-leverage premise used in the other proposals in this same batch, leaving the predicted sign unjustified.

An outer RANK on a rank product is a monotone transformation that leaves the portfolio sort (and hence the ls_alpha evidence) essentially unchanged, so apart from shortening the trend window from 5y to 3y this is a cosmetic re-run of the archived MarginErosionUnderThinCash rather than a substantively different mechanism.

The cost-growth-minus-sales-growth wedge is close to the classic Abarbanell–Bushee fundamental-signals literature so the first leg is not new, but the interaction with cash-to-current-liabilities is coherent, correctly signed, and coverage-friendly, making it a legitimate if incremental test.

Multiplying an unranked 0–3 loss count by a rank forces every non-loss firm (the large majority of the cross-section) to exactly zero, so the signal degenerates into a tie-heavy loss-count indicator in which the gross-margin leg has no effect over most of the sample, and both legs individually restate the well-known profitability/gross-profitability anomalies.

The numerator is deflated by liabilities while the denominator is deflated by revenue, so the ratio is dimensionally incoherent across capital structures, and dividing by a three-year volatility that can be arbitrarily close to zero makes the score explosive and effectively a low-earnings-volatility (known anomaly) proxy that 1% winsorization only partially tames.

This is a single-leg re-run of the archived CashRunwayShortfall's cash/cogs component with dlc netted out, and as a plain net-cash-to-costs level it is largely a restatement of the well-documented cash-holdings/net-debt return anomaly rather than a new cross-theme interaction.

Debt-maturity structure is a genuinely untouched dimension in this archive and its interaction with margin volatility is an economically well-specified rollover-risk mechanism with a sign consistent with the expression; the main caveat is undefined/noisy values for near-zero-debt firms, which should be screened.

This is an additive recombination of two legs already in the archive rather than a new mechanism, and the two legs work against each other mechanically because VOL of (pi+dp)/lt scales with the magnitude of coverage itself, so NEG(VOL) tilts toward low-coverage, low-profitability firms and partially cancels the trough-coverage leg.

Economically coherent and internally consistent (both legs point negative), but it is a two-component swap on ThinEbitdaCoverageWithDebtBuildup that recycles WorstYearCashCoverage as leg one, and leg two is close to the well-documented net debt issuance/change-in-leverage anomaly, so it reads as an incremental variant rather than a new cross-theme idea.

Peak-relative fundamental drawdown is a genuinely distinct deterioration construct from the level and trend measures already tested, the sign logic is consistent (larger drawdown × higher liability burden → lower returns), though the reviewer should watch for the point mass at zero when the current year is its own 3-year max and for the fact that the un-normalized drawdown is dominated by high-variance, high-level coverage firms.

The claim that the depreciation-intensity leg is "untouched by the archive" is false — CollateralShieldedLiquidityGap used dp/at with the opposite economic sign (capital intensity as pledgeable collateral, i.e., protective) — so the proposal's expected sign is a coin flip against an already-tested contrary story, and dp/cogs is largely an industry capital-intensity sort layered on a standard net-leverage sort.

Cash-flow-to-total-debt is a textbook published distress/solvency ratio and this is also a denominator-and-tax tweak of the archived WorstYearCashCoverage, with the added hazard that near-zero (dlc+dltt) firms produce explosive values that 1% winsorization will not fully tame.

Cash share of current assets is a liquidity-composition dimension genuinely distinct from the che/lct levels already tested, and scaling current liabilities by the operating cost base is a defensible claim-pressure normalization, though the lct/cogs leg is ambiguous since high payables can also reflect available trade credit rather than pressure.

A coherent, correctly signed additive combination of the archive's only FMB-bearing leg (cash-earnings coverage) with its highest-alpha leg (net short-term funding of operating assets), and the additive form is a substantive design change rather than a cosmetic variant since it preserves cross-sectional dispersion instead of concentrating it in one rank-product tail.

This is the same economic content as the companion proposal in the exact rank-product form that has already produced near-zero FMB slopes in roughly ten archived signals, so it is a functional-form duplicate whose answer is largely pre-known and adds little beyond the additive version.

The supplier-credit-stretching channel is a genuinely untested angle and the sign logic is internally consistent, but lct also contains short-term debt so the "payables" reading is loose, lct appears in both legs (mechanically correlating them and weakening the conditional interpretation), and rising current liabilities is a working-capital accrual component whose published sign points the opposite way — a tension the proposal should address.

This is essentially the product of two canonical published anomalies — expense/asset growth (CMA) and low profitability (RMW) — which the reasoning itself concedes, so it is a rediscovery whose most likely outcome is a raw-return slope with an FF5-spanned alpha.

The first leg is verbatim the archived WorstYearCashCoverage signal and the second is the well-documented liability-growth/debt-issuance anomaly already used in ThinEbitdaCoverageWithDebtBuildup, so this is a low-information recombination of existing components rather than a new mechanism.

Asset turnover is a legitimately new quality dimension for this archive with a consistent sign, but sales/assets and liabilities/assets are two of the five Altman Z-score inputs so the construct is close to a known distress-score rediscovery, and low turnover may proxy for capital intensity (i.e., collateral, already tested via dp/at) rather than idle capacity.

The nested SUMRANK does not implement the stated symmetric three-symptom score — it weights the coverage leg 50% and the other two 25% each — and the construct is otherwise an incremental bolt-on to the archive's existing WeakCoverageWithFundingGapAdditive whose third leg (payables stretch) already showed a null FMB slope, so any gain is likely arithmetic rather than informational.

A single, well-isolated substitution (current-year cash-earnings coverage → worst-of-three-years) inside the archive's best-performing aggregation, motivated by the only construct with |FMB t|>2; it is incremental and the trough numerator sits awkwardly against a current-year liability denominator, but it tests a genuine downside-state measurement question rather than a cosmetic reweighting.

Revenue-growth volatility is the one instability channel the archive has not used and is economically upstream of the margin- and coverage-volatility legs already tried, though the reviewer notes it overlaps materially with the published fundamental-volatility/information-uncertainty literature and should be judged on incremental content over that baseline.

This is the archive's ShortTermFundedAssetsThinMargin with the rank-product swapped for SUMRANK — identical economic content, and the archive already demonstrates (product coverage+gap ≈ 0 FMB vs additive coverage+gap = -1.77) that additive aggregation lifts the cross-sectional slope, so the result is largely predictable and the test is a functional-form rediscovery rather than a new hypothesis.

Industry neutralization is a legitimately untested design dimension and a plausible diagnosis for the alpha/FMB divergence, but the proposal changes two things at once (aggregation form and industry adjustment) relative to the archive's rank-product original, so the result will be unattributable unless run alongside a controlled baseline.

Applying a three-year moving average to both legs of an existing archive signal is a smoothing variant, not a new mechanism, and it duplicates the timing-refinement question already posed by the trough-coverage proposal while sacrificing coverage and freshness of information.

The nested weighting is internally consistent and combines the three legs that actually carried the archive's cross-sectional and portfolio evidence, but it is fundamentally a mechanical ensemble of two already-tested composites sharing the same dominant leg, so incremental information is likely modest.

Replacing symmetric growth dispersion with a one-sided peak-relative shortfall is a substantively different economic state (demand hole versus uncertainty), the sign direction matches the expression, and it is not a rediscovery of an archived or standard published anomaly, though the ratio's denominator (revt) will be unstable for very small-revenue firms.

This is a pure denominator swap (act to cogs) on the archived leader with the partner leg held fixed — a cosmetic scaling variant rather than a new mechanism, and the claim that it reduces overlap with liquidity-composition results is weak since dlc−che dominates either normalization.

Shortening the archived leader's 3-year volatility to a one-year absolute growth is a lag-window variant, and the symmetric |growth| leg conflates the well-known asset/sales-growth anomaly (high growth → low returns) with the intended instability channel, so a confirming result would be uninterpretable.

COGS growth is nearly collinear with revenue growth for most firms, so this is a near-duplicate of the archived VolatileTopLineWithFundingGap leader dressed in a cost-side story, and the stated demand-versus-treasury decomposition cannot be identified from two such correlated volatility measures.

The expression is internally inconsistent with its hypothesis — SUB(wcap, che) equals non-cash current assets *minus current liabilities*, not "inventory and receivables," so high values indicate a conservatively funded working-capital position whose natural return direction is the opposite of the stated negative sign (and contradicts the archived NEG(wcap/at) result).

The nesting does deliver the claimed equal 25% weights and the four legs are economically distinct, but this is largely an ensemble-stacking extension of the archived gen-6 composite (gap+vol+trough, alpha −0.059/t −4.55) with one extra leg, so the expected gain is incremental and dilution of the strongest leg (downside asymmetry, alpha −0.067) is a real risk.

This is a single-leg substitution (trough coverage → margin downside asymmetry) inside the already-tested FundingGapWithInstabilityAndTroughCoverage structure with identical 50/25/25 weights, making it a cosmetic variant whose only differentiator from Proposal 1 is leg weighting rather than a new mechanism.

Swapping pretax-margin asymmetry for gross-margin asymmetry is a defensible operating-vs-below-the-line attribution test and the sign logic is internally consistent, but it remains a one-variable perturbation of the archive's best signal and the archive already shows gross-margin-based legs (MarginErosionUnderThinCash, ShortTermFundedAssetsThinMargin) behave similarly, limiting the informational payoff.

The change in short-term debt share as a creditor-revealed distress footprint is a genuinely new channel relative to the archive's static maturity-share test, the partner leg avoids the (dlc−che)/act crowding that saturates the rest of the archive, and the sign is coherent — the main risks are denominator instability for near-zero-debt firms and noise in a one-year delta.

The tail-of-the-burn-distribution construction is internally consistent (TS_MIN picks the worst drawdown, NEG orients it toward distress) and generalizes the working downside-tail principle to the cash process, though it partly re-uses che on both legs and is close in spirit to the already-tested CashBurnWithNearTermClaims.

A legitimate attribution test with correct sign orientation, but the decomposition is incomplete — it substitutes only the cash component of (dlc−che)/act while never testing dlc/act alone, so a null result cannot cleanly separate "cash scarcity" from "rollover debt," and −che/act is itself close to the published cash-holdings characteristic.

This is a pure re-weighting of three legs already tested in FragilityIndexFourLeg, EarningsDownsideAsymmetryWithFundingGap and DownsideAsymmetryWithCashOnly, so it is a cosmetic weighting variant rather than a new mechanism, and the claim that it will "convert" the leader's weak FMB slope by adding a 25%-weight leg is not credible since the vol leg's own slope (-2.5) was obtained in a different pairing.

Same objection as the previous proposal — it substitutes one already-tested archive leg (trough coverage) for another (revenue vol) inside an identical nested SUMRANK, which is an attribution exercise on weights rather than a substantively different signal, and the two candidates are near-duplicates of each other.

Applying the downside-tail transform to the coverage ratio instead of the margin is a real mechanism change and the expression matches the hypothesis, though it overlaps meaningfully with CoverageDrawdownUnderLeverage (peak-relative coverage decline) and risks inheriting that signal's mediocre alpha since (pi+dp)/lt asymmetry is largely a scaled version of pi-margin asymmetry when lt is stable.

Retained-earnings flow is a genuinely unused channel in this archive and the construction is internally consistent, but the reviewer should note that DELTA(re) is close to net income less dividends and RE/assets is a classic Altman Z-score input, so partial rediscovery of the profitability/distress-score literature is a live risk.

The test is confounded — it simultaneously changes the liquidity denominator (act to lct) and adds a three-year TS_MIN, so a change in alpha versus DownsideAsymmetryWithCashOnly cannot be attributed to the tail transformation, and che/lct in various forms has already appeared in five archive signals.

A clean, well-motivated ablation that completes the (dlc−che)/act decomposition the archive left half-finished and whose sign convention is internally consistent; it is diagnostic rather than novel, so its value depends entirely on the follow-up being drawn from the outcome rather than on the signal itself.

This is a cosmetic variant of the already-evaluated VolatileTopLineWithFundingGap — replacing the current net short-term funding gap with its own three-year maximum, a highly persistent balance-sheet ratio whose rolling max is near-collinear with its level — so it cannot deliver economically new information about either channel.

The (dlc−che)/act leg in the already-evaluated VolatileTopLineWithFundingGap is dominated by the same −che scaling, so this is essentially the archive's existing pair with dlc dropped, and the same "cash-only substitution" diagnostic has already been run once (DownsideAsymmetryWithCashOnly) with a predictable outcome.

The mean-to-trough gap of a three-observation growth series is nearly a monotone transform of that series' standard deviation, so the "asymmetry" leg is not economically distinct from the already-tested VOL(GROWTH(revt,1),3) leg — the hypothesis claims a downside-versus-dispersion distinction the expression cannot actually separate at a three-year window.

All three legs and both pairwise combinations are already in the archive (FragilityIndexFourLeg, DownsideAsymmetryWithCashOnly, VolatileTopLineWithFundingGap), so this is purely a re-weighting exercise — exactly the kind of cosmetic reshuffle that generates apparent improvement through weight-fitting rather than new economic content.

This is a genuine, economically motivated repair of a documented failure mode (the cash-only denominator's right skew and wrong-signed FMB slope) that stays in a distinct single-ratio functional family, though it should be checked that firms with negative gross profit do not produce a negative denominator and flip the ratio's sign for precisely the distressed names of interest.

TroughCoverageFundingGapAdditive already pairs the identical trough-coverage leg with (dlc−che)/act, and since that gap is largely driven by the −che term this proposal is the same signal with dlc removed rather than a new complementarity; note also that three of the six proposals in this batch perform the same "swap the funding gap for −che/act" move.
